episode_title: Everyday Neuro 029: Remembering the Future - Prospective Memory, Healthy Ageing, and the Power of Co-Design

real_qa.q: What is prospective memory and how does it differ from retrospective memory?
real_qa.r: Prospective memory is the ability to remember an intention and carry it out at the right moment in the future, often described as remembering to remember. Unlike retrospective memory, which involves remembering things that have already happened (like what you had for breakfast), prospective memory is about remembering the future. It functions like the brain's built-in reminder system, allowing us to remember to attend appointments, take medication, or call a friend on their birthday.

real_qa.q: What brain regions are involved in prospective memory and how do they work together?
real_qa.r: Prospective memory involves multiple brain systems working together like an orchestra. The prefrontal cortex acts as the prospective memory manager, holding onto your to-do list. Brodmann's Area 10 (frontopolar cortex) is especially large in humans and helps with cognitive branching, allowing us to keep a future intention active while focusing on something else. The hippocampus enables us to remember the intention itself, while the parietal cortex helps direct attention and notice when the right cue or trigger has appeared.
real_qa.requete: prospective memory brain regions prefrontal cortex hippocampus

real_qa.q: What is the age prospective memory paradox and why does it occur?
real_qa.r: Laboratory studies show older adults perform worse than younger adults on prospective memory tasks, yet in everyday life, older adults sometimes perform as well or even better than younger adults. This paradox occurs because older adults often develop effective compensatory strategies, may be more conscientious about important intentions, and a 2004 meta-analysis by Julie Henry and colleagues revealed that age-related declines happen in lab conditions but real-world performance did not show such decline.
real_qa.requete: age prospective memory paradox older adults

real_qa.q: What is co-design and how has Maria Arbarnugo used it in her prospective memory research?
real_qa.r: Co-design involves bringing researchers and the people affected by the research together so they are actively involved in shaping the research and developing solutions collaboratively. In Maria's research, this has involved working with older adults in group sessions to discuss their experiences of prospective memory failures, introducing three strategies to overcome them, and asking older adults to help develop instructions that are easy to understand and use in daily life, ensuring the research is grounded in their actual experiences.
real_qa.requete: co-design older adults prospective memory research

real_qa.q: What psychological and social factors influence whether people follow through on their intentions?
real_qa.r: Forgetting to do something is not just about having a poor memory. Motivation plays a big role—how important something is to us, how motivated we are to carry it out, and whether we see it as a priority all influence whether we actually follow through. Additionally, social context matters: everyday intentions do not happen in isolation but often involve other people, our routines, and the environments we are in, which can either support or challenge our prospective memory.
real_qa.requete: prospective memory motivation social context factors

Her work emphasizes incorporating the voices and lived experiences of the populations she studies rather than relying solely on laboratory findings.
